report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that soursop (graviola; *Annona muricata*) cures cancer in humans is **not supported by reliable clinical evidence**.

**What supports the idea:** Laboratory and animal studies report that soursop extracts and compounds called acetogenins can inhibit or kill cancer cells, including pancreatic-cancer cells. This is a legitimate early research signal, but results in cell cultures or animals do not establish a safe, effective human treatment; dose, absorption, toxicity, and effects on tumors and survival can differ greatly in people.  
https://edrn.cancer.gov/data-and-resources/publications/22475682-2053-graviola-a-novel-promising-natural-derived-drug-that-inhibits-tumorigenicity-and-metastasis-of-pancreatic-cancer-cells-in-vitro-and-in-vivo-through-altering-cell-metabolism/  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36139697/

**What weighs against the claim:** Cancer Research UK reports no valid human clinical trials demonstrating graviola treats cancer. Memorial Sloan Kettering likewise says there is no proof of benefit for cancer patients. Therefore, it cannot accurately be called a cure.  
https://www.cancerresearchuk.org/about-cancer/treatment/complementary-alternative-therapies/individual-therapies/graviola  
https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/graviola

There are also safety concerns with concentrated leaf/seed teas or supplements: Annonaceae-plant consumption has been associated with an atypical Parkinsonism syndrome in Caribbean populations, though this association does not by itself prove causation. Soursop products may also affect blood pressure or interact with treatment.

Eating the fruit as food is different from taking high-dose extracts, but neither should replace evidence-based cancer care. A person with cancer should discuss any soursop product with their oncology team before using it.
